metadata.title: 1970 Case 48
metadata.original_presentation: A 45-year-old woman was admitted to the hospital because of a changing cardiac murmur.

required.content: What is the patient's past medical history related to cardiac issues?
required.response: At the age of 17 years she had been informed that she had a heart murmur. No restrictions were imposed upon her, and she underwent two eventful pregnancies at 23 and 26 years of age.

teaching_points.content: A heart murmur detected in adolescence can be benign or indicative of underlying cardiac pathology. Regular follow-up is important.

required.content: What symptoms did the patient experience prior to admission?
required.response: Ten years before admission she began to have episodes of pallor and cyanosis of the hands on exposure to cold. Eight months before entry she was informed that she had hypertension. Three months before admission exertional dyspnea and fatigue developed, and she began to experience episodes of 'heaviness' in the anterior portion of the chest.

teaching_points.content: Symptoms such as exertional dyspnea and chest heaviness can indicate worsening cardiac function.

required.content: What is the patient's family history of cardiac conditions?
required.response: Her mother had hypertension and had had several myocardial infarcts. Eleven siblings were living and well, without known heart disease or hypertension.

teaching_points.content: Family history of hypertension and myocardial infarction can increase the risk of similar conditions in the patient.

current_ideal_differential_diagnosis.name: Mitral Valve Prolapse
refuting_evidence: no specific mention of mitral valve prolapse symptoms like palpitations or syncope
additional_information_needed: echocardiogram to assess valve structure and function

current_ideal_differential_diagnosis.name: Aortic Stenosis
refuting_evidence: no mention of syncope or classic triad of symptoms

current_ideal_differential_diagnosis.name: Pulmonary Hypertension
refuting_evidence: no specific mention of right heart failure symptoms

current_ideal_differential_diagnosis.name: Coronary Artery Disease
refuting_evidence: no mention of typical angina or risk factors like diabetes or smoking

current_ideal_differential_diagnosis.name: Raynaud's Phenomenon
key_features: pallor and cyanosis of hands on cold exposure
supporting_evidence: episodes of pallor and cyanosis of the hands on exposure to cold
refuting_evidence: does not explain cardiac murmur or chest heaviness

required.content: What were the findings on physical examination?
required.response: The patient was thin but appeared well and was not cyanotic. There was a slight malar flush. Very prominent A waves, with smaller V waves, were observed in the jugular veins. The lungs were normal. There was a slight systolic impulse over the left parasternal region, and a presystolic impulse was felt in the right hypochondrium. Prominent protodiastolic (S3) and presystolic (S4) gallop sounds were heard low along the left sternal border, becoming louder on inspiration. The second heart sound was slightly split on inspiration and narrowed on expiration; the pulmonic component was slightly increased. A systolic ejection murmur was heard along the lower left sternal border and was Grade 3 on inspiration and Grade 1 on expiration; no diastolic murmur was heard. The abdomen was normal. The peripheral pulses were full, equal and without delay; there was no edema, cyanosis or clubbing of the extremities.

teaching_points.content: Prominent A waves in the jugular venous pulse can indicate right atrial pressure increase, often due to tricuspid stenosis or pulmonary hypertension.

current_ideal_differential_diagnosis.name: Pulmonary Hypertension
key_features: prominent A waves in jugular venous pulse
increased pulmonic component of second heart sound
supporting_evidence: prominent A waves in jugular veins
increased pulmonic component of second heart sound
systolic ejection murmur along the lower left sternal border
additional_information_needed: Echocardiogram to assess pulmonary artery pressure

current_ideal_differential_diagnosis.name: Mitral Valve Stenosis
supporting_evidence: prominent A waves in jugular veins
history of heart murmur since age 17
additional_information_needed: Echocardiogram to assess mitral valve function

current_ideal_differential_diagnosis.name: Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy
supporting_evidence: family history of cardiac issues (mother with myocardial infarcts)
refuting_evidence: no evidence of left ventricular hypertrophy on physical exam
additional_information_needed: Echocardiogram to assess for left ventricular hypertrophy

current_ideal_differential_diagnosis.name: Atrial Septal Defect (ASD)
key_features: fixed splitting of second heart sound
supporting_evidence: prominent A waves in jugular veins
refuting_evidence: second heart sound split is not fixed

required.content: What were the results of the laboratory tests?
required.response: The hematocrit was 43.9 per cent; the white-cell count was 10,000, with 80 per cent neutrophils, 1 per cent band forms, 15 per cent lymphocytes and 4 per cent monocytes. The erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 42 mm in one hour, and the prothrombin time was 14.6 seconds, with a control of 12.9 seconds. The creatinine was 1.2 mg, the conjugated bilirubin 0.8 mg, the total bilirubin 1.3 mg, the iron 86 μg, and the protein 6.6 g (the albumin 3.9 g, and the globulin 2.7 g) per 100 ml. The sodium was 141 mEq, the potassium 3.8 mEq, the chloride 97 mEq, and the carbon dioxide 28 mEq per liter. Tests for antinuclear antibody, rheumatoid factor and cryoglobulins and an L.E.-cell test were negative. Serum immunoelectrophoresis and agarose-gel electrophoresis were negative.

teaching_points.content: Normal creatinine and electrolyte levels suggest preserved renal function, which is important in managing cardiac patients.

required.content: What were the findings on the electrocardiogram and imaging studies?
required.response: An electrocardiogram showed a normal rhythm at a rate of 85, with normal PR and QRS intervals; the axis was +30°; the P waves were peaked in Leads 2, 3, aVF, V2 and V3, and there was generalized lowering of the T waves, with a tendency to low voltage of the QRS complexes. A vectorcardiogram was interpreted as consistent with right atrial enlargement and right ventricular hypertrophy. X-ray films of the chest disclosed that the heart was not enlarged in the transverse diameter, although it encroached upon the retrosternal space; the aortic arch was in a normal position on the left side; the lungs and pulmonary vasculature appeared normal.

teaching_points.content: Right atrial enlargement and right ventricular hypertrophy on ECG can indicate pulmonary hypertension or valvular heart disease.

current_ideal_differential_diagnosis.name: Pulmonary Hypertension
key_features: prominent A waves in jugular venous pulse
supporting_evidence: prominent A waves in jugular venous pulse
systolic ejection murmur along the lower left sternal border
refuting_evidence: normal pulmonary vasculature on chest X-ray
additional_information_needed: echocardiogram to assess pulmonary artery pressures
right heart catheterization for definitive diagnosis

current_ideal_differential_diagnosis.name: Tricuspid Valve Disease
supporting_evidence: prominent A waves in jugular venous pulse
additional_information_needed: echocardiogram to evaluate tricuspid valve structure and function

current_ideal_differential_diagnosis.name: Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy
refuting_evidence: normal heart size on chest X-ray
additional_information_needed: echocardiogram to assess for left ventricular outflow tract obstruction

current_ideal_differential_diagnosis.name: Rheumatic Heart Disease
supporting_evidence: history of heart murmur since age 17
refuting_evidence: negative tests for antinuclear antibody, rheumatoid factor, and cryoglobulins
additional_information_needed: echocardiogram to assess for valvular damage

required.content: What management steps were taken upon hospital admission?
required.response: An operation was performed on the second hospital day.

teaching_points.content: Surgical intervention may be necessary in cases of significant valvular heart disease or structural cardiac abnormalities.
